answers.primary: A PostToolUse hook in the project's checked-in .claude/settings.json with matcher "Edit|Write", whose command reads .tool_input.file_path from the hook's stdin JSON and runs the formatter on exactly that file (the documented shape is `jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write`). Narrow it to TypeScript with a per-handler `if` field such as "Edit(**/*.ts)" so the process only spawns on matching calls.
answers.rejected_alternative: Project guidance in CLAUDE.md or a .claude/rules/ file, which is what is already in place. It is instruction text that shapes what Claude tries to do but does not change what Claude Code actually does, so it cannot guarantee the step.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code fires PostToolUse itself after each matching tool call, so the formatter runs whether or not the model remembered to format.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs as a separate OS subprocess with the event JSON on stdin, outside the model's context window. Nothing of the formatter's work enters the conversation unless the hook writes it back deliberately (stderr on a block, or additionalContext), so the model's context stays clean.
answers.lifecycle: Fires after every successful Edit or Write tool call, in every session started in that repo once the settings file is committed, including tool calls made inside subagents. It stops applying if the hook entry is removed or if disableAllHooks is set.
answers.failure_mode: It misses TypeScript files Claude creates through Bash (a heredoc, sed, a codegen script), because the matcher only sees Edit and Write; the documented fix is a Stop hook that scans `git status --porcelain` once per turn, or an additional Bash matcher. PostToolUse also cannot undo the edit, and if the formatter binary is missing the hook exits with a non-zero code that is not 2, so the action proceeds with only a hook-error notice: it fails open on formatter breakage.
answers.version_caveat: No plan restriction; PostToolUse hooks are generally available. Writing the matcher as "Edit,Write" instead of "Edit|Write" requires Claude Code v2.1.191 or later, and the `if` field works only on tool events (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied).

answers.primary: permissions.deny rules in the repo's checked-in .claude/settings.json: Read(.env), Read(.env.*) and Read(secrets/**), plus matching Edit(...) entries for the same paths. Deny rules are evaluated first by Claude Code, before ask and allow, and a deny in project settings cannot be re-allowed by a teammate's user or local settings.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook on the file tools that inspects .tool_input.file_path and exits 2. It works and is the documented pattern for protected files, but it is a script every teammate must keep functioning, and it fails open whenever the script errors, while a deny rule is evaluated unconditionally by the harness.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model, so no prompt or CLAUDE.md text can loosen them.
answers.context_boundary: Evaluated inside the Claude Code process before the tool runs, so the file contents never reach the model's context window. A scoped rule such as Read(secrets/**) leaves the Read tool visible and returns a denial to the model, whereas a bare-name deny such as Read would strip the tool from context entirely.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from session start for every session started in the repo and for every read attempt for the life of the session. Deny and ask rules are not gated by the workspace trust dialog (only allow rules and additionalDirectories are), so a teammate gets the restriction on their first run with no acceptance step; it stops only if the rules are deleted from the file.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for Claude's built-in file tools and for file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash such as cat, head, tail and sed, and symlink tricks are covered because a deny matches either the link path or its target. It does not reach an arbitrary subprocess: a Python or Node script the agent writes can still open .env, so pair it with OS-level sandboxing (sandbox.filesystem.denyRead) if the requirement is real containment rather than tool-level refusal.
answers.version_caveat: A Read deny rule also blocks the Edit tool on the same path only on Claude Code v2.1.208 or later, so include explicit Edit(...) deny entries for older clients. As of v2.1.210 only Read(path) and Edit(path) rules are consulted in file permission checks: a Write(secrets/**), NotebookEdit(...) or Glob(...) path rule is accepted, never used, and produces a startup warning.

answers.primary: A Notification hook in ~/.claude/settings.json (or shipped fleet-wide as a plugin) with matcher "permission_prompt", running the platform notifier: osascript display notification on macOS, notify-send on Linux, a PowerShell message box or toast on Windows. Add a second entry with matcher "idle_prompt" if 'Claude is done and waiting for your next prompt' should also alert.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that fires a notification before every tool call. It would alert continuously rather than only when the run is actually blocked, since it cannot tell which calls will prompt and which are auto-approved.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness fires the event and runs the command; the model has no part in it and cannot suppress or trigger the alert.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs as a subprocess in the developer's own OS session, outside the model's context window: the notification event JSON goes in on stdin and nothing comes back into the conversation. Notification is one of the events where exit code 2 cannot block anything, so the hook is purely a side effect.
answers.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code emits a notification of the matched type, for the life of every session once the hook is in user settings. It stops when the hook entry is removed or hooks are disabled, and it never fires for a run that is not actually waiting.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory: it can raise the alert but cannot make anyone respond, and delivery failures are silent. On macOS osascript routes through Script Editor, which silently drops notifications until that app is granted notification permission once, and in an SSH session or container there is often no desktop notification bus at all, so notify-send just errors while the run stays blocked unseen.
answers.version_caveat: The permission_prompt and idle_prompt matchers are generally available. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers, which cover background sessions, require Claude Code v2.1.198 or later and fire only while agent view is open, so they are not a substitute for the terminal-session case.

answers.primary: permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode set to "disable" (and permissions.disableAutoMode alongside it if auto mode is also out of scope) delivered as managed settings by MDM: the macOS com.anthropic.claudecode managed preferences domain, the Windows HKLM policy key or C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json, /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json, /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json, or server-managed settings.
answers.rejected_alternative: The same key placed in the developer's own ~/.claude/settings.json. The setting is honored from any scope, but the developer owns that file, so it only locks out someone who wants to be locked out and fails the 'cannot lift it from their home directory' requirement.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Managed settings sit at the top of the settings precedence chain and are evaluated by Claude Code at startup, above command line arguments.
answers.context_boundary: Enforced in the CLI process at startup and at any attempted mode switch; nothing about the policy reaches the model's context window. Because managed settings outrank CLI flags, --dangerously-skip-permissions, --allow-dangerously-skip-permissions and --permission-mode bypassPermissions are refused rather than merged.
answers.lifecycle: Read when the process starts (and re-fetched in the background for server-managed settings) and enforced for the whole session; a session that was already in bypass mode terminates with the SessionEnd reason bypass_permissions_disabled. It stops applying only when the device stops receiving the policy.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed inside Claude Code, since no user, project, local or CLI scope can override a managed setting and a lower scope cannot re-allow what a higher one denies. The weak point is delivery rather than evaluation: a developer with local administrator rights can edit the policy file or registry hive, so protect those paths with OS permissions, prefer the HKLM hive over HKCU, and consider forceRemoteSettingsRefresh so startup fails closed when the policy cannot be fetched.
answers.version_caveat: The legacy Windows location C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json stopped being read in v2.1.75 and must be migrated to C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode, or the policy silently does nothing. forceRemoteSettingsRefresh and policyHelper are managed-settings-only keys, server-managed delivery and the organization-wide admin toggles are Team and Enterprise plan features, and WSL only inherits the Windows policy chain when wslInheritsWindowsSettings is set.

answers.primary: A Stop hook of type "command" that checks for evidence the suite ran and passed during this turn (for example a marker file with the session id and turn timestamp, written by a PostToolUse hook on Bash when the test command exits 0) and returns {"decision": "block", "reason": "..."} when that evidence is absent, so Claude is sent back to keep working.
answers.rejected_alternative: An agent-type Stop hook that spawns a subagent to run the suite itself. It removes the marker plumbing, but agent hooks are explicitly experimental, cost a model call plus a full test run at every turn end, and return a judgment rather than a recorded exit code.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the outcome: Claude Code decides whether the turn may end, and the model only reacts to the reason string it is handed. The model forgetting to test is precisely what this removes from the model's hands.
answers.context_boundary: The hook is a subprocess receiving the Stop event JSON (including stop_hook_active and last_assistant_message) on stdin, outside the model's context window. Only the reason string, or hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext, crosses back into the conversation, so the turn resumes with a short instruction rather than raw test output unless the hook chooses to include it.
answers.lifecycle: Fires every time the main agent finishes responding, not only when work is genuinely complete, and applies until the turn is allowed to end. It must read stop_hook_active and exit early when true, or it will keep blocking a condition that will never resolve.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open at the edges: Claude Code overrides the hook after 8 consecutive blocks and ends the turn anyway, Stop hooks do not fire on user interrupts (an API error fires StopFailure instead), and any exit code other than 2 from a crashed script or a missing jq lets the turn finish with only a hook-error notice. It also fires on purely conversational turns, so the check has to tolerate turns where nothing was edited or it becomes noise.
answers.version_caveat: Stop hooks are generally available and need no flag; raise the eight-block ceiling with the CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP environment variable if convergence legitimately needs more iterations. Agent-type hooks are experimental and may change, and /goal is a built-in session-scoped prompt Stop hook if you want the judgment-based variant without writing configuration.

answers.primary: An ask rule, "Bash(git push *)" in permissions.ask, placed in managed settings (or project settings) so it loads regardless of session configuration, with a parallel "PowerShell(git push *)" entry where that tool is in use. Ask rules are evaluated before allow rules and are one of the few things that still force a prompt under bypassPermissions and auto mode.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask" for git push. It achieves the same prompt, but adds a script and a process spawn on every Bash call for something the permission system expresses in one line, and a hook's decision is merged with sibling hooks rather than being authoritative.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code raises the prompt itself; the model cannot answer it, argue past it, or mark it 'don't ask again'.
answers.context_boundary: The prompt is raised in the user's terminal by Claude Code and the human's answer stays in the harness; the model sees only the resulting tool result (the push happened, or it was denied). The rule itself never enters the model's context, so no prompt injection can reason it away.
answers.lifecycle: Applies to every matching Bash or PowerShell call for the life of every session that loads the settings file. It is never consumed: unlike an allow prompt it cannot be answered with 'Yes, don't ask again', so it fires every single time until the rule is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed in interactive sessions, but the guarantee is only as strong as the pattern. Claude Code checks each subcommand of a compound command and deny/ask rules match past leading environment assignments, yet a wrapper script, a git alias, or /usr/bin/git push sidesteps a literal 'git push *' pattern. In dontAsk mode there is no prompt to show so the call is denied instead, and in headless -p runs there is no human present to confirm at all.
answers.version_caveat: No version gate on ask rules themselves. The mode interactions are the thing to verify: bypassPermissions and auto still honor content-scoped ask rules, sandboxing's autoAllowBashIfSandboxed substitution does not suppress them, and a PreToolUse hook returning "allow" cannot suppress them either, which is exactly why this holds under any approval configuration.

answers.primary: A hook pair on the Bash tool deployed through managed settings: a PreToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" that appends .tool_input.command plus session_id, cwd and a timestamp to the audit sink, and PostToolUse plus PostToolUseFailure hooks that record the outcome. Use type "http" to POST to a central audit service rather than a local file when the record must survive the developer's machine.
answers.rejected_alternative: Instructing the model to log what it ran, via CLAUDE.md or a skill. That is self-report, exactly what the requirement rules out, and it is least reliable in the cases compliance cares about.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code invokes the hook with the exact tool_input it is about to execute, independent of anything the model says it did.
answers.context_boundary: The hooks run outside the model's context window, receive the tool call JSON on stdin, and write to a file or HTTP endpoint without returning anything to the conversation. The model is never told the audit exists and cannot shape or suppress the record.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool call in every session on machines carrying the managed policy, including calls made inside subagents (the input carries agent_id and agent_type). It stops only if the managed hook entry is removed, since disableAllHooks in user, project or local settings cannot disable a managed hook.
answers.failure_mode: PreToolUse records intent, so a command later blocked by a deny rule still appears in the log, and PostToolUse alone would miss failed commands, which is why PostToolUseFailure is paired with it. Coverage is per tool call, not per process: whatever a shell script or make target spawns internally is invisible, the separate PowerShell tool needs its own matcher, and a log file on the audited developer's own disk is writable by them, so ship it off-box.
answers.version_caveat: Set allowManagedHooksOnly to true in managed settings so no user, project or unvetted plugin hook can run alongside; that key is managed-settings-only, and hooks from plugins force-enabled in managed enabledPlugins remain exempt. For HTTP delivery, allowedHttpHookUrls and httpHookAllowedEnvVars constrain the destination and the interpolated secrets, and non-2xx responses, connection failures and timeouts on an HTTP hook are non-blocking errors, so records can be lost silently.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook with matcher "Bash" that parses the command and returns permissionDecision "deny" for any aws invocation that is not exactly `aws s3 ls`, paired with a permissions.allow rule "Bash(aws s3 ls)" so the one approved call runs without a prompt. The hook supplies the exception logic that permission rules structurally cannot express.
answers.rejected_alternative: Permission rules alone: deny "Bash(aws *)" with allow "Bash(aws s3 ls)". Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and specificity does not change that order, so the broad deny swallows the narrow allow. The documentation states outright that a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions, so this configuration blocks aws s3 ls too.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness for both halves: Claude Code runs the hook and applies the allow rule. The model never sees the policy, only the refusal reason.
answers.context_boundary: The hook subprocess receives the full command string on stdin and decides outside the model's context window; only permissionDecisionReason crosses back so Claude learns why the call was refused and can stop retrying. Deliberately keeping any `Bash(aws *)` deny rule out of settings is what lets the allow rule reach the approved call at all.
answers.lifecycle: Runs before every Bash tool call for the life of the session, in every permission mode including bypassPermissions and dontAsk, since PreToolUse fires before the permission-mode check. It applies until the hook entry is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for what the script recognizes and open for what it does not: the script must itself handle compound commands, $( ) and backtick substitution, /usr/bin/aws, `env AWS_PROFILE=x aws ...`, `xargs aws`, and `bash -c "aws ec2 ..."`, because matcher filters by tool name only and the optional `if` filter is best-effort and fails open on commands it cannot parse. A crashed hook, or any exit code other than 2 with no JSON on stdout, drops the call back into the normal permission flow.
answers.version_caveat: PreToolUse hooks and the allow/deny/ask permissionDecision values are generally available with no plan gate; the fourth value "defer" exists only in headless -p runs behind an Agent SDK wrapper. If you implement the guard as a prompt-type hook instead, note that from v2.1.210 a denial ends the turn by default unless you set continueOnBlock to true.

answers.primary: Enable OS-level sandboxing: sandbox.enabled true with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, or the equivalent sandbox.credentials.files entries with mode "deny", set in managed (or user) settings. Sandboxing is the only layer that constrains the Bash tool's child processes, and the restriction applies to all subprocesses including children of children.
answers.rejected_alternative: More Read(...) deny rules, which is what is already in place. Those cover Claude's built-in file tools and the file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, but the documentation is explicit that they do not apply to arbitrary subprocesses like a Python or Node script that opens the file itself.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness sets the boundary and the OS enforces it (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus a seccomp filter on Linux and WSL2), so the block holds even against a process the model never reasoned about.
answers.context_boundary: Enforcement lives in the kernel around the spawned process tree, entirely outside the model's context window; the model sees only a permission-denied error from whatever it ran. Read and Edit deny rules are merged into the same sandbox boundary, so the tool-level and OS-level layers compose rather than compete.
answers.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command and its descendants from session start for as long as the setting is present. It stops applying for anything matched by sandbox.excludedCommands and for calls that use the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open in two default configurations worth closing: if the sandbox cannot start, commands run unsandboxed with only a warning unless failIfUnavailable is true, and the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter stays available unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is false. Blocking those paths also breaks legitimate work, so expect git over SSH and any aws CLI call to start failing and plan the allowRead exceptions accordingly.
answers.version_caveat: Sandboxing is macOS, Linux and WSL2 only, defaults to disabled, and has no native Windows equivalent, so a Windows fleet needs a different control. sandbox.credentials.files requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later, and filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly (managed settings only) is what stops a developer re-opening the path in their own settings, since denyRead merges from all scopes but allowRead would otherwise merge too.

answers.primary: strictPluginOnlyCustomization set to true in managed settings, which locks exactly the four surfaces named (hooks, skills, agents, mcp) to plugin-provided or managed sources, combined with strictKnownMarketplaces to pin the marketplace, extraKnownMarketplaces to pre-register it, and enabledPlugins in managed settings to force-enable the IT plugins.
answers.rejected_alternative: Shipping the same components as a plugin and asking everyone to install it, without the managed lock. Plugin distribution is purely additive: a developer's ~/.claude/skills/, a repo's .claude/agents/, project settings hooks and a project .mcp.json would all still load beside the sanctioned plugin.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code decides which sources it discovers and loads at startup; managed settings are the top precedence tier and cannot be overridden.
answers.context_boundary: Discovery and loading happen in the CLI process before the session exists, so a blocked skill, agent, hook or MCP server never enters the model's context at all: its instructions and tools are absent rather than present-and-refused. Only the plugin-provided and managed components contribute anything to the context window.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated when Claude Code loads configuration at session start and on configuration refresh, and it governs the whole session; the marketplace restriction is additionally enforced on marketplace add and on plugin install, update, refresh and auto-update. It stops applying only when the device stops receiving the managed policy.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the four locked surfaces, but coverage is exactly those four: slash commands, output styles, CLAUDE.md and .claude/rules/ are not locked by this key, so repo-committed instruction text still reaches the model. Add allowManagedHooksOnly and allowManagedMcpServersOnly as reinforcement, and expect support load when developers' existing personal skills and agents silently stop loading with no per-item explanation.
answers.version_caveat: strictPluginOnlyCustomization is readable only from managed settings and takes either true or an array such as ["skills", "hooks"]; unrecognized surface names are ignored rather than failing the file, so newer names are safe to add early. Close the per-run bypass with disableSideloadFlags, which rejects --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config at startup and requires Claude Code v2.1.193 or later.
